researchAttemptsAppend: 30 September renewed official-source/general-definition review: Recovered USDA’s official 23 December 2013 Curaçao FAIRS report (CB1317). researchAttemptsAppend: 30 September renewed official-source/general-definition review: Recovered the official TCI Plant Health Services Division fruit-and-vegetable conditions PHSD 4001/1, revised 14 January 2014, through the German federal plant-health authority. Its personal/domestic exception waives only the import permit and still requires a phytosanitary certificate; it is not textually baggage-only but concerns fruit/vegetables, not manufactured tea. It supplies neither a tea waiver nor a valid reason to impose fruit certification on sencha. Re-reading the Ordinance revealed a material difference from KN/VC: plant includes a part without an express living qualifier, and regulated article paragraph (a) separately names packaging/containers without the trailing capability/deemed wording. Sections 34–35 require written prior permits for covered articles; 2024 regulation 27 expressly includes mail/courier and certificate attachments. Applying the manufacturing-risk exclusion alone therefore does not resolve every local coverage route. Treating every clean package as automatically permit-required would also overread context; the unresolved issue is this operative scope/section 36 conditions, not merely lack of a tea-named letter.
remainingQuestion: Current section 36 processing/import conditions or legally grounded scope of nonliving plant parts and clean packaging. The actual manufactured-tea evidence resolves the scientific category but does not unambiguously settle the additional statutory classes. The separate 2016 food-law private-consumption exception remains favorable with its previously recorded commencement limitation.
